note: Reference densities for interpolating a volume conversion where a Form has no direct density source of its own (§5.3). A figure taken from here is tagged densitySource: "estimated" and carries the tilde and dotted underline wherever it appears. Density never touches a stored amount — it is a display convenience over weight, so an estimate here cannot corrupt a figure the site presents as authoritative.
howToUse: Prefer a measured figure from the ingredient's own USDA record: `node scripts/data/usda.ts fetch <fdcId>` reports the household portions that record publishes, and those are measured, not estimated. Reach for a class only when the record has none.

sources.USDA FDC: Household portion weights published on the food's own record. Public domain.
sources.King Arthur Baking: Ingredient weight chart, used where USDA publishes no household portion for a common baking ingredient.
sources.physical: Standard density of the substance at room temperature.

classes.label: Flour and finely milled powders
classes.reference: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, bleached
classes.note: Scooped rather than spooned-and-levelled. Flour is the ingredient where volume measuring goes most wrong — a heavy hand can put 20% more in the same cup, which is the reason this project authors in grams.

classes.label: Granulated sugar and similar free-flowing crystals
classes.note: USDA's granulated sugar record publishes no household portion, so this comes from the standard baking reference.

classes.label: Icing sugar and other very fine powders
Cocoa and other light milled powders
Fresh leafy herbs, whole leaves
classes.note: Whole leaves, loosely packed. Chopped is roughly twice as dense — the same record gives 2.65 g per tablespoon chopped, which works out near 42 g per cup.

classes.label: Dried leafy herbs
classes.note: Crumbled leaf. The same record gives 4.5 g per tablespoon for the ground form, which is more than twice as dense — use the ground-spice class for anything milled.

classes.label: Ground spices
classes.note: Ground spices vary by a factor of about two across the shelf — cinnamon is dense, dried oregano is not. Treat this as a floor for confidence, and prefer the ingredient's own record.

classes.label: Flaked and coarse salt
classes.note: This is the one figure here that changes the outcome of a dish. Coarse salts differ by brand by more than a factor of two — Morton kosher is about 4.8 g per teaspoon against Diamond Crystal's 2.8 — which is exactly why salt is authored by weight and never by spoon.

classes.label: Dried pasta shapes
classes.note: The weakest class here, and worth saying so: the same record gives 64 g per cup for shells and 122 g for elbows. A cup of pasta is not a quantity. Show weight and treat any volume figure as a rough orientation.

classes.label: Rolled oats and flakes
classes.note: USDA's rolled oats record publishes no household portion.

classes.label: Chopped, slivered or ground nuts
classes.reference: Nuts, almonds — slivered 108 g, ground 95 g, sliced 92 g per cup
classes.note: Averaged across the cut forms on one record, which agree closely enough for a display conversion.

classes.label: Water, stock and thin watery liquids
classes.note: Stock, wine and vinegar sit within a percent or two of this, which is well inside the precision a kitchen can act on.

classes.label: Milk, cream and pourable dairy
classes.note: Cream is slightly lighter than milk, not heavier — the fat it carries is less dense than the water it replaces.

classes.label: Cooking oils
classes.note: Common cooking oils run between about 0.91 and 0.93, so one figure serves them all at display precision.

classes.label: Honey, treacle and heavy syrups
classes.note: Half again as heavy as water, which is why a syrup measured by volume rather than weight is a common way to get a bake wrong.

classes.label: Butter and solid fats
classes.note: A US stick is 113 g, so a cup is two sticks.
